verbalization: Escitalopram, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), is shown to affect multiple biological pathways that ultimately contribute to the development of Denture stomatitis. The evidence suggests that escitalopram influences BR serine/threonine kinase 1, a gene product that is involved in the expression of Zinc finger protein 471 (EZFIT-related protein 1), which in turn may play a role in the pathogenesis of the condition. Similarly, escitalopram is linked to the activation of Wnt family member 6, which is encoded by a gene involved in cholesterol metabolism. These pathways collectively appear to be involved in the inflammatory and cellular dysregulation characteristic of Denture stomatitis. The overlapping involvement of escitalopram in multiple distinct biological processes, each potentially contributing to the condition, supports the hypothesis that escitalopram may have a role in its development. The integration of these pathways highlights the complexity of the mechanism by which escitalopram may influence the disease, emphasizing the need for further investigation into the precise molecular interactions involved.
